blocks.content: The dns-resolution-flow topic showed an authoritative server finally providing the real answer at the end of the chain. This topic looks at exactly what that answer actually is, and the several different KINDS of answers a DNS server can actually provide, depending on the specific question being asked.

DNS is not only about looking up a website plain IP address. An authoritative server holds several different types of records, each one answering a genuinely different kind of question about a domain.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576024-146441182.png
1. A Record: The Most Common Lookup
blocks.text: 1. A Record: The Most Common Lookup

blocks.content: An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, exactly the lookup traced through in full detail in the resolution flow topic. This is the single most common type of DNS record, and the one people usually picture when they think about DNS lookups at all.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576025-89629272.png
blocks.alt: A Record: The Most Common Lookup

blocks.content: 2. AAAA Record: The IPv6 Equivalent

An AAAA record does exactly the same job as an A record, but returns an IPv6 address instead of an IPv4 one, directly tying back to the ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic from the earlier module. A single domain commonly has both an A and an AAAA record at once, letting devices connect using whichever protocol version they actually support.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576025-494550383.png
3. CNAME Record: An Alias Pointing to Another Name
blocks.text: 3. CNAME Record: An Alias Pointing to Another Name

blocks.content: A CNAME record does not return an IP address at all, it returns ANOTHER domain name instead, an alias. If www.example.com has a CNAME record pointing to example.com, then a lookup for www.example.com actually gets redirected to look up example.com instead, whose own A record then provides the final actual IP address.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576025-641253447.png
blocks.alt: CNAME Record: An Alias Pointing to Another Name

blocks.title: Why this is genuinely useful
blocks.content: If the underlying IP address ever needs to change, updating just the ONE A record for example.com automatically updates the effective address for every single CNAME alias pointing at it too, no need to update each alias individually.

4. MX Record: Where Email Should Actually Go
blocks.text: 4. MX Record: Where Email Should Actually Go

blocks.content: An MX, mail exchange, record specifically tells the rest of the internet which mail server is responsible for handling email sent to a given domain. When someone sends an email to you@example.com, the sending mail server looks up example.com MX record specifically to find out exactly where to actually deliver that message.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576026-772930637.png
blocks.alt: MX Record: Where Email Should Actually Go

blocks.content: 5. TXT Record: Arbitrary Text Information

A TXT record holds arbitrary text information attached to a domain, not addressing information at all. Real, common uses include proving ownership of a domain to an outside service, publishing email security and anti spam policies, and various other verification and configuration purposes that need to attach some piece of text to a domain in a way anyone can look up.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576026-679259634.png

blocks.title: A genuinely widespread real use
blocks.content: Nearly every service that asks you to verify domain ownership, adding a website to a search console, connecting a custom domain to a hosting provider, does it by asking you to add a specific TXT record, proving you control the domain DNS settings.
6. NS Record: Delegating Authority

An NS, name server, record specifically points to the actual authoritative name servers responsible for a domain, directly tying back to the dns-hierarchy topic delegation structure. This is exactly the mechanism that lets one level of the DNS tree point down to whichever specific servers are responsible for the next level.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576026-772672734.png
7. Different Needs, Different Record Types

A browser loading a website needs an A or AAAA record. An email server trying to deliver a message needs an MX record. A service verifying you actually own a domain might check for a specific TXT record. Every one of these is a genuinely different kind of question, and DNS records are exactly how a single domain can answer all of them, each with its own dedicated record type.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576026-640936827.png

blocks.title: One domain, many simultaneous record types
blocks.content: A single domain like example.com commonly has an A record, an AAAA record, several MX records, a TXT record or two, and NS records, all existing at once, each answering its own specific kind of question independently.

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

items: Assuming DNS only ever returns IP addresses, when several genuinely different record types exist, each answering a different kind of question.
Confusing a CNAME record, which points to another domain name, with an A record, which points directly to an IP address.
A records and AAAA records provide IPv4 and IPv6 addresses respectively.
CNAME records create aliases that resolve through another domain name.
MX records route email delivery, TXT records hold arbitrary verification text, and NS records delegate authority to specific name servers.
